label: Intro
title: How Tagalog sentences work
summary: The big ideas, explained in plain English before any rules
goals: Know what a subject and a predicate are, in plain words
See how Tagalog arranges a sentence differently from English
Meet the small joining words (markers and linkers) that hold sentences together
Learn the colour code used everywhere in Tagalify

sections.title: Who or what is it about?

blocks.t: Every sentence has two halves. One half is **who or what the sentence is about**. The other half is **what we say about it**.
Grammar books call these the **subject** and the **predicate**. You do not need to remember the words. You only need to spot the two halves.

head: Half
Plain meaning
English example
rows: who or what we are talking about
what we say about it: an action, a description, or what it is
blocks.title: Two halves of a sentence

blocks.t: A predicate can be an action (is eating), a description (is big), or an identity (is a teacher). Whatever it is, it tells us something about the subject.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.t: Say any English sentence in your head, such as "My brother is tired." Ask: who is it about? (my brother) What is said about him? (is tired). You just found the subject and the predicate.
In English the subject nearly always comes first: "The house is big." Tagalog can say it that way, but in everyday speech it usually puts the **predicate first**.

blocks.title: The same idea in both languages
blocks.note: Word for word: big the house. There is no word for "is" in this order.

blocks.title: Tap a sentence to hear it
Remember
items: In everyday speech, Tagalog sentences usually start with the action or description.
The person or thing it is about comes after, with a small marker word in front.

sections.title: The kinds of word you will meet

blocks.t: These plain-English labels are all you need. Each has its own colour in Tagalify, so you can see how a sentence is built at a glance.

What it does
Example

blocks.title: The colour code

blocks.t: English has little words such as "the" and "a". Tagalog has **markers**, and they do more work. A marker sits in front of a noun and tells you the noun's job in the sentence.
In these lessons a noun does one of three jobs: it is **what the sentence is about**, it is an **owner**, or it is a **place or direction**.

head: Job
For things and places
For one person's name
Example
rows: ang báhay **ng** laláki, ang báhay **ni** Maria
**sa** báhay (in, at or to the house)
blocks.title: Markers at a glance
blocks.note: You do not have to learn all of these now. Lessons 4, 6 and 8 teach them one step at a time.

blocks.title: The key rule
blocks.t: A noun that the sentence is about is always preceded by its marker, except when you speak to someone directly or give a command. In English you can say "Peter is good". In Tagalog you need the marker: **Mabaít si Peter**.
In English we put a describing word right in front of a noun: "big house". Tagalog adds a small piece of **glue** between them, called a linker.

blocks.title: Gluing a describing word to a noun
blocks.note: malakí + -ng + báhay is written malakíng báhay. Lesson 7 explains exactly which linker to use.

blocks.title: Why linkers exist
blocks.t: The linker has no meaning of its own. It simply tells the listener that the two words are closely related and that one describes the other.

English does this too. The pronoun "I" becomes "me" or "my" depending on its job. Tagalog also changes pronouns by job. For example, **akó** means "I" as the subject, while **ko** means "my" after a noun.

blocks.title: One idea, different shapes
blocks.note: Lesson 6 covers the subject pronouns and Lesson 8 covers the "my, your" forms.

blocks.title: A surprise for English speakers
blocks.t: Tagalog has **two** words for "we". One includes the person you are talking to and one leaves them out. You will meet them in Lesson 6.
To show more than one, Tagalog puts **mga** (said ma-nga) in front of the noun. Unlike English, it does not change the noun itself.
Notice that the describing word **malilínis** (from malínis) also changed shape to show more than one. Lesson 4 explains how.
Finally, Tagalog speakers show respect with the little word **pô**. It has no meaning of its own. It simply makes a sentence politer, like adding "sir" or "madam" in English. Lesson 3 teaches it.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.t: Politeness is part of grammar in Tagalog. Using pô with older people and people in authority shows good manners.
Each lesson has three steps. You can do them in order, and your progress is saved on this phone.

head: Step
What you do
rows: Read the lesson one page at a time. Tap any Tagalog word or sentence to hear it.
Meet the lesson's new words. Each one joins your daily review.
Answer questions: pick, listen, build sentences and match. Missed ones come back.

blocks.title: Study tips
items: Short and often beats long and rare. Ten minutes a day is a good habit.
Say each word out loud after you hear it.
Open the Review tab daily. Spaced review brings words back just before you forget them.
The small guide under a word (like ma-gan-DA) shows which syllable to stress.

blocks.title: Accent marks and the sound guide
blocks.t: Words are written with the textbook's accent marks (malakí, báhay), which show the stress. In the sound guide, **capital letters** show the stressed syllable and **Q** stands for the glottal catch, a tiny stop in the throat like the break in "uh-oh". Lesson 2 explains both.

exercises.q: In "The dog is good", which part is the predicate?
exercises.explain: The predicate says something about the subject. "The dog" is the subject.

exercises.q: In everyday Tagalog, which part usually comes first?
options: The thing the sentence is about
exercises.explain: Tagalog usually puts the predicate first: Malakí ang báhay.

exercises.q: Which of these is a marker?
exercises.explain: Ang is a marker. Báhay is a noun and malakí describes something.

exercises.q: Which marker goes before a person's name when the sentence is about them?
exercises.explain: Si is used before names: Mabaít si Peter.

exercises.q: In "ang báhay ng laláki", what does ng show?
exercises.explain: Ng means of: the house of the man.

exercises.q: Which marker shows a place or direction?
exercises.explain: Sa means in, at, on or to.

options: Joins two words when one describes the other
exercises.answer: Joins two words when one describes the other
exercises.explain: Linkers like -ng and na are the glue in malakíng báhay.

exercises.q: Which Tagalog word means "we" when you include the person you are talking to?
exercises.explain: Táyo includes the listener. Kamí leaves them out.

exercises.q: In "Malakí ang báhay", which word is the predicate?
exercises.explain: Malakí (big) is what is said about the house.

exercises.q: What does the little word pô add?
exercises.explain: Pô means roughly sir or madam.
Malakí ang báhay means The house is big.

exercises.q: Match each marker to its job.

recap: A sentence has a subject (who or what it is about) and a predicate (what is said about it).
Tagalog usually puts the predicate first: Malakí ang báhay.
Markers (ang, si, ng, ni, sa, mga) sit before nouns and show their job.
Linkers (-ng, -g, na) join describing words to nouns.
Pronouns and some words change shape, and pô adds respect.
